title: Lazy eye (amblyopia) in children
intro: Amblyopia, often called lazy eye, is reduced vision in one eye because the brain does not learn to use it properly during childhood. The eye itself may look normal. If found early, treatment is usually successful, so vision screening in young children is valuable.

sections.heading: What causes it
paragraphs: Amblyopia develops when the brain favours one eye. Causes include a squint where the eyes point in different directions, a big difference in focusing power between the eyes, or something blocking the vision such as a cloudy lens. The brain suppresses the blurred or misaligned image, and vision in that eye does not develop properly.

sections.heading: How it is recognised
paragraphs: Children rarely complain because they do not know how they should see. Signs include a turned eye, tilting the head, squinting, poor depth perception or closing one eye in bright light. Vision screening tests in infancy and before school are designed to find it. If you suspect a problem, ask for an eye test.

sections.heading: Treatment
paragraphs: First, any needed glasses are prescribed and worn consistently, since this alone improves vision in many children. If vision remains weaker in one eye, the stronger eye is covered with a patch for some hours a day, or blurred with eye drops, to make the brain use the weaker eye.

Treatment works best when started before about seven to eight years of age, but older children can still benefit. It requires patience and encouragement; rewards, games and drawing while patching can help. Skin irritation from patches can be eased by changing brands or caring for the skin.

sections.heading: Squint surgery and follow-up
paragraphs: Some squints are treated with surgery on the eye muscles, which improves alignment but does not by itself cure amblyopia. Regular check-ups monitor progress, and vision may need maintenance treatment until the child is older, as it can slip back.

sections.heading: Helping your child
paragraphs: Explain in simple terms why the patch or glasses are important. Involve nursery or school, keep appointments and praise effort. Untreated amblyopia can lead to permanent reduced vision, so do not wait if you are worried.

examples.title: Making patching easier
examples.text: Imagine your five-year-old dislikes the eye patch. You could set a regular time when they play with a favourite game, use sticker charts and ask the eye clinic about alternatives like drops.

examples.title: Spotting early signs
examples.text: Suppose you notice your toddler sometimes turns one eye inward in photographs. You might request an eye examination rather than waiting for them to grow out of it.
